title: Cozy Stories to Fall Asleep To 🌙 6 Calm Tales for a Peaceful Night | Snortlo
intro: Hello, and welcome. This is Snortlo, and tonight I have six gentle stories to keep you company as you drift off. Before we begin, take a moment to get comfortable. Let your shoulders drop. Dim the lights, or turn them off altogether. Pull the blanket up a little higher. There is nothing you need to do now, and nowhere you need to be. You don't have to follow every word, and you certainly don't need to stay awake until the end. If you fall asleep halfway through, that's the whole idea. Take a slow breath in. And let it go. Let's begin.

stories.title: The Midnight Laundromat
stories.text:
On the corner of a quiet street, between a shoe repair shop and a bakery that closed at six, there was a laundromat that never closed at all. Its sign said Bluebell Wash and Fold, and one of the letters flickered, just a little, as if it were blinking slowly at the night.

Ruth worked there from ten in the evening until six in the morning. She had worked there for eleven years, and in that time she had come to know the machines the way some people know their neighbors. Number four was gentle and a little slow. Number nine liked to hum a low note when it was spinning. The big dryer at the end, the one everyone called the bear, made a soft thumping sound, like someone patting a pillow over and over.

Tonight it was raining. Not a storm, just a steady, patient rain that ran down the big front windows in thin silver lines. The streetlights made little golden circles on the wet pavement, and every now and then a car went by with a sound like a long, slow breath.

Inside, everything was warm. The laundromat always smelled of clean cotton and soap, with a faint sweetness from the dryer sheets. Ruth kept a kettle in the back room, and she made herself a cup of chamomile tea, and she sat on the tall stool behind the counter, and she listened to the machines.

The first visitor of the night was a man named Theo. He came in at a quarter to midnight carrying a quilt so large that he had to hold it with both arms, and even then the corners dragged along the floor. It was a patchwork quilt, faded blue and yellow and green, with little stitched stars in some of the squares.

"Good evening," said Ruth.

"Good evening," said Theo, a little out of breath. "I'm told the big one at the end can handle this."

"The bear," said Ruth, nodding. "She can handle anything."

Theo fed the quilt into the big washer, one fold at a time, as carefully as if he were tucking it into bed. He explained that his grandmother had made it, that it had been on his bed for many years, and that his cat had recently decided to sleep on it after walking through a flowerpot. He said this with a small, tired smile, as though the cat had done it on purpose and he had decided to forgive her.

Then he sat down in one of the plastic chairs by the window and watched the quilt go round and round, and after a while his eyes began to close.

Ruth didn't mind. People often fell asleep in the laundromat. There was something about the sound of the machines, the soft roll of the water and the gentle clunk of a button against the drum, that made the world feel slower. She turned the radio down a little, so that the quiet music from the late night station was only just there, like the memory of a song.

At half past midnight, a young woman came in with a backpack and a laundry bag the size of a small sofa. Her name was Pip, or at least that was what was written on the bag in marker. She was a student, and she had brought a thick book about clouds, and she sat cross-legged on the folding table while her clothes washed, reading about the puffy ones and the flat gray ones and the long, thin clouds that look like brushstrokes.

Every so often she would look up from the book and out at the rain, as if checking that the clouds were still doing what the book said.

Ruth brought her a cup of tea without being asked. Pip looked surprised, then pleased, then held the cup in both hands and breathed in the steam.

"Is it always this quiet?" Pip asked.

"Mostly," said Ruth. "Sometimes there's a little rush around two. People who can't sleep. People who just finished a late shift. People who forgot they had nothing clean for tomorrow."

"Which one are you?" asked Pip.

Ruth thought about it. "I think I'm the one who keeps the kettle on," she said.

By the wall near the door there was a corkboard, and on the corkboard there was a sign that Ruth had made years ago. It said, Lost Socks, Looking for Their Partners. Underneath it, held up with little pushpins, were socks of every kind. A striped red one. A tiny white baby sock with a lace edge. A thick wool sock the color of oatmeal. A sock covered in small cartoon pineapples.

Sometimes, someone would come in, look at the board, and gasp, and take down a sock, and hold it up next to the one they had been carrying in their coat pocket for weeks. Ruth always counted those as good nights.

Tonight, while Pip was folding her shirts, she wandered over to the board and stopped. Then she unzipped the front pocket of her backpack and took out a sock covered in small cartoon pineapples.

She held the two socks side by side. They were a perfect match.

"I've been carrying this around since the summer," she said quietly, as though it were a secret.

"Well," said Ruth, "it seems it's been waiting for you."

Pip rolled the two socks together into a neat little ball and tucked them into her bag, and for the rest of the night she looked very pleased with herself.

At about one o'clock, the big washer finished, and Theo woke with a small start and blinked around, unsure for a moment where he was. Then he remembered, and he moved the quilt into the bear, and set the dial to low, and sat back down. The dryer began its slow, soft thumping, pat, pat, pat, like a heartbeat, and within a few minutes he was asleep again, his chin resting on his chest.

The rain kept falling. Pip finished her folding, put on her coat, and stood in the doorway for a moment, looking out at the wet street. Then she waved to Ruth and stepped out into the night, her hood up, the bag of clean clothes bumping gently against her back.

Ruth wiped down the folding table. She swept the small drifts of lint from under the dryers. She straightened the stack of old magazines on the windowsill, the ones about gardens and boats and beautiful kitchens that nobody had ever cooked in.

When the bear finally stopped, the quilt came out warm and soft and smelling of nothing at all, which is the very best thing a quilt can smell of. Theo held it against his chest like a sleepy child, and he thanked Ruth, and he said he would see her again, probably the next time the cat had an adventure.

After he had gone, the laundromat was very still. There was only the hum of the lights and the soft patter of rain on the window.

Ruth made another cup of tea. She sat on her tall stool, and she looked at the row of clean, quiet machines, and she listened to the rain.

Outside, the street was empty and shining. Somewhere far off, the first gray light was beginning, very slowly, to think about the morning.

But that was still hours away. For now, there was only the warmth, and the tea, and the softly blinking sign, and the rain, falling and falling, gently, over everything.

stories.title: The Lighthouse Keeper and the Captain
stories.text:
At the far end of a small fishing town, past the last row of painted houses and the little harbor where the boats knocked softly together, there was a lighthouse. It was white with a red stripe around its middle, and it stood on a round shoulder of rock with the sea on three sides.

The light itself did not really need a keeper anymore. It turned on by itself every evening and off by itself every morning. But the town liked having someone there, and so for many years the lighthouse had been looked after by a man named Mr. Pell.

Mr. Pell was tall and a little stooped, with a gray beard and a knitted hat that he wore in every season. He polished the brass. He painted the railings. He wrote down the weather in a thick blue notebook, every single day, in small careful handwriting. Wind from the west, light. Sky mostly clear. Sea calm, slightly grumpy in the afternoon.

He also had a seagull.

Or rather, the seagull had him. It had arrived one spring, landed on the railing outside the kitchen window, looked at Mr. Pell for a long time with one round yellow eye, and then decided to stay. Mr. Pell named it the Captain, because it stood very straight and seemed to believe it was in charge of everything.

The Captain had opinions. He had opinions about the weather, about the tide, about the boats in the harbor, and most of all about Mr. Pell.

Each morning, Mr. Pell would open the kitchen window, and the Captain would be there, waiting. Mr. Pell would say good morning, and the Captain would tilt his head and make a short, sharp sound, which Mr. Pell had decided meant, you are late.

"I am not late," Mr. Pell would say. "The sun is early."

The Captain would ruffle his feathers, unconvinced.

This particular day began with fog. It came in soft and white from the sea, rolling over the rocks and wrapping itself around the lighthouse until the whole world was just a pale, glowing blanket. The foghorn down on the point gave its long, low note, once every half minute, like a big animal sighing in its sleep.

Mr. Pell liked foggy days. Everything was quieter. The gulls in the harbor stopped shouting. The waves sounded far away, hushed and polite. He made himself a pot of strong tea and a bowl of porridge with brown sugar, and he sat at the kitchen table with his notebook.

Fog, he wrote. Thick and friendly.

The Captain tapped on the window with his beak.

Mr. Pell opened it, and the cool, damp air came in, smelling of salt and seaweed. The Captain looked at the porridge. Then he looked at Mr. Pell. Then he looked at the porridge again.

"It's not for you," said Mr. Pell. "You don't even like porridge. You told me so last Tuesday."

The Captain made a small noise that might have been an objection and might have been a sneeze.

Mr. Pell sighed and put a spoonful of oats on the windowsill. The Captain examined them, pecked at one, and then turned away and looked out at the fog, as if to make it very clear that he had only done it to be polite.

After breakfast, Mr. Pell put on his old wool coat and went up to paint the railing on the gallery, the narrow balcony that ran all the way around the top of the tower. It was slow work. He had a small tin of white paint and a brush with soft bristles, and he moved along the railing a little at a time, humming to himself.

The Captain supervised.

He walked along the part of the railing that was not yet painted, keeping just ahead of the brush. Every so often he would stop and look back at Mr. Pell's work with an expression that seemed to say, you missed a bit.

"I did not miss a bit," Mr. Pell told him. "I am coming back for that bit. That bit is part of the plan."

The Captain did not look convinced. He seldom did.

By midday, the fog had begun to thin. Little holes opened in it, and through them Mr. Pell could see patches of blue water, glittering, and once, a small red fishing boat drifting home with its engine puttering softly. The foghorn grew quieter, and then it stopped altogether, and the sudden silence felt like a held breath being gently let go.

Mr. Pell sat down on the top step to rest. The Captain sat beside him, at a polite distance, and together they watched the fog lift off the sea like steam rising from a cup of tea.

"You know," said Mr. Pell, "the light doesn't really need me."

The Captain looked at him.

"It turns itself on. It turns itself off. It doesn't need anyone to wind it or polish it or tell it what time it is. I suppose I'm here mostly for the company."

The Captain shifted his feet on the warm stone. He looked out at the harbor, and then back at Mr. Pell, and then he made a sound that was softer than any sound Mr. Pell had ever heard from him. A low, short chuckle, almost.

Mr. Pell decided that meant, me too.

In the afternoon, the sun came out properly, and the whole coast lit up. The rocks were wet and shining. The grass along the cliff path bent and swayed in a mild breeze. Down in the harbor, someone was hanging washing on a line, and the white sheets lifted and fell like slow sails.

Mr. Pell finished the railing. It gleamed. He stepped back to admire it, and the Captain walked along it from one end to the other, inspecting every inch, and when he reached the end, he turned around, looked at Mr. Pell, and gave one short nod.

Mr. Pell felt unreasonably proud.

The evening came slowly, the way it does by the sea. The sky turned pale gold, and then apricot, and then a soft and dusty pink. The water went from blue to silver to a deep, quiet violet. The boats in the harbor turned on their little lamps, one by one, like a row of fireflies settling down for the night.

And at exactly the right moment, the light at the top of the lighthouse woke up.

It began to turn, slow and steady, sending its long beam out over the darkening water, around and around, the way it had every night for a hundred years. It swept across the rocks, across the harbor, across the roofs of the little painted houses, and out to the horizon, where the first stars were coming out.

Mr. Pell sat at his kitchen window with a cup of cocoa. The Captain stood on the sill outside, tucked up against the glass where it was warm, his feathers fluffed, his eyes half closed.

Mr. Pell opened his blue notebook one last time.

Evening clear, he wrote. Sea calm. Railing painted. The Captain approves.

Then he closed the notebook, and turned down the lamp, and sat for a while in the soft dark, listening to the waves breathing on the rocks below, and watching the great slow light go round, and round, and round.

stories.title: The Night Baker
stories.text:
Nora's alarm went off at two in the morning, the way it always did, with a soft little chime that sounded like a spoon tapped against a teacup. She did not mind getting up at two. She had been doing it for so long that the middle of the night felt like her own private morning.

She lived above her bakery, in a small apartment with slanting ceilings and a window that looked out over the main street of a sleepy town. She dressed in the dark, pulled on her thick socks and her flour-dusted cardigan, and went down the narrow back stairs, one creaking step at a time.

The bakery kitchen was cool and dark and smelled faintly of yesterday's bread. Nora switched on the lights, one row and then another, and the room woke up around her. The long wooden table. The tall shelves of flour and sugar in big glass jars. The mixer in the corner, solid and patient as an old dog. And the oven, wide and black, waiting.

The first thing she always did was turn on the oven. The second thing was put the kettle on. The third thing was switch on the little radio on the windowsill, very low, so that it played soft piano music, the kind that seems to drift in from another room.

Then she looked out the window.

It was snowing.

Not heavily. Just a few big, slow flakes drifting down past the streetlamp, turning gold as they passed through its light and then white again as they settled on the windowsills and the roofs of the parked cars. The street was empty and blue and very, very quiet.

Nora smiled. She loved baking on snowy nights. Everything felt tucked in.

She had set the dough for the bread the evening before, and it had been rising slowly all night in big covered bowls on the cool shelf at the back. She lifted the cloth from the first bowl, and there it was, soft and round and puffed up like a sleeping cat. She pressed one finger gently into it, and the little dent filled back in, slowly. Perfect.

She turned the dough out onto the floured table and began to shape the loaves.

This was her favorite part. There was a rhythm to it. Fold, press, turn. Fold, press, turn. The dough was cool and smooth and alive under her hands. She shaped round loaves and long loaves and little rolls the size of a fist, and laid them in rows on wooden boards, and covered them with linen cloths to rest.

While they rested, she made the cinnamon buns.

She rolled out a big sheet of sweet dough, brushed it with melted butter, and scattered it with brown sugar and cinnamon until the whole kitchen smelled like a warm hug. Then she rolled it up into a long spiral, cut it into thick slices, and placed each one into a buttered tin, snug against its neighbors.

By half past three, the kitchen had begun to warm up. The windows fogged a little at the corners. The radio played something slow on a cello. Nora took a sip of her tea, which had gone lukewarm, and didn't mind at all.

The first loaves went into the oven at four. She slid them in on a long wooden paddle, one after another, and closed the heavy door. Within a few minutes, the smell began. That deep, golden, toasty smell of bread baking, which is surely one of the kindest smells in the world.

At a quarter past four, there was a soft knock at the back door.

Nora knew who it would be. She opened the door, and there stood Walt, the street sweeper, in his orange coat and his woolly hat, with snow on his shoulders and a pink nose from the cold.

"Morning, Nora," said Walt.

"Morning, Walt," said Nora. "You're early."

"It's snowing," said Walt, as if that explained everything, and in a way it did.

Walt swept the main street every morning before the town woke up. He had done it for years. And every morning, at about this time, he stopped at the back door of the bakery, and Nora gave him the first roll out of the oven and a cup of coffee, and he stood in the warm doorway and ate it slowly while the snow fell behind him.

He never asked for it. She never charged him for it. It was simply what happened, the way the sun coming up is simply what happens.

Tonight she handed him a cinnamon bun instead of a roll, still far too hot to really hold, and Walt juggled it from hand to hand and laughed softly, and blew on it, and took a careful bite.

He closed his eyes.

"Well," he said, after a while. "That's the best one yet."

"You say that every time," said Nora.

"It's true every time," said Walt.

They stood together in the doorway for a few minutes, not saying much. Watching the snow. Listening to the radio. The alley was white and untouched, and the only footprints in it were Walt's, leading up to the door.

Then Walt finished his coffee, handed back the cup, tipped his woolly hat, and went off down the street with his wide broom, sweeping a neat dark path through the snow, the sound of the bristles soft and steady. Shh. Shh. Shh.

Nora went back inside.

The rest of the early morning passed in a gentle blur of work. Loaves came out of the oven golden and crackling, and she set them on the cooling racks, where they made tiny popping sounds as they settled. Bakers call this the bread singing. The cinnamon buns came out sticky and glossy, and she drizzled them with a little white icing. She filled the front counter with baskets of rolls and trays of buns and a row of small apple tarts, each one with a lattice top like a tiny woven blanket.

By six, the sky outside had turned from black to a deep, soft blue. The snow had stopped. The whole street was covered in a fresh, smooth layer of white, except for Walt's neat swept path down the middle, like a ribbon.

Nora unlocked the front door. She turned the little sign around. She wiped her hands on her apron and looked at her bakery, warm and golden and full of good things, and she felt the particular quiet happiness of a job done slowly and well.

The bell above the door gave its small, cheerful ring as the first customer of the day came in, stamping snow from their boots, and breathing in deeply, and smiling.

Upstairs, the little apartment was waiting, and soon Nora would climb the creaking stairs and curl up under her heavy quilt, while the town went about its morning below.

But not yet. For now, there was bread on the shelves, and snow on the roofs, and the whole sleepy world smelled, just faintly, of cinnamon.

stories.title: The Cat Who Ran Elm Lane
stories.text:
At the edge of a small town there was a short, curving street called Elm Lane. It had seven houses on it, and it was run, quietly and very efficiently, by a cat.

The cat was gray, with white paws and a white tip on the end of her tail, as if she had once dipped it in milk. She had a great many names. At the blue house on the corner, she was called Biscuit. At the yellow house with the porch swing, she was called Duchess. At the house with the vegetable garden, the old gentleman called her Mrs. Whiskers, very formally, and always tipped his hat to her.

She answered to all of them. Or rather, she answered to none of them, but she allowed them all.

Every house on Elm Lane believed, privately, that the cat belonged to them. And the cat, privately, believed that Elm Lane belonged to her.

Her day began at sunrise, on the low stone wall at the end of the street. She sat there with her paws tucked under her and watched the light come up over the rooftops, turning the chimneys pink and the windows gold. She watched the first lamps come on in the kitchens. She listened to the first kettles begin to whistle. This was, as far as she was concerned, her morning meeting. She was taking attendance.

Once she was satisfied that everyone was awake and accounted for, she began her rounds.

The first stop was the blue house on the corner, where a young family lived. There was a small girl named Rosie who ate her breakfast by the window, and every morning the cat sat outside on the sill and looked at Rosie's toast with great seriousness. Rosie would open the window and offer her a corner of it, and the cat would sniff it, and decline, because she did not care for toast. But it was important that the offer was made. It showed good manners.

Then she went next door, to the yellow house with the porch swing, where Mrs. Lowe lived. Mrs. Lowe was retired, and she did the crossword puzzle on the porch every morning with a cup of milky coffee. The cat would climb up onto the swing beside her and sit very still while Mrs. Lowe read out the clues.

"Seven letters," Mrs. Lowe would say. "A cozy place to sleep."

And the cat would yawn, enormously, and Mrs. Lowe would laugh and say, "Yes, I suppose that's the answer to everything with you, isn't it."

The cat stayed long enough for the swing to rock her nearly to sleep, and then she hopped down, because there was work to be done.

The third house belonged to the old gentleman with the vegetable garden, whose name was Mr. Abbott. He spent his mornings among his tomatoes and his beans, and the cat spent her mornings supervising him. She sat at the end of the garden path, between the rows of lettuce, and watched him tie up the bean plants with little bits of string. Whenever he stood up to stretch his back, she blinked at him slowly, which, in the language of cats, means, you are doing very well.

"Thank you, Mrs. Whiskers," Mr. Abbott would say, and tip his hat.

By late morning, the sun had warmed the street, and the cat moved on to the most important part of her day. This was the inspection of the sunny spots.

There were a great many sunny spots on Elm Lane, and they moved throughout the day, which required careful management. At eleven, the best one was on the front step of the green house, where the stone had been warming since dawn. At noon, it was on the hood of the old car parked outside the house with the red door. At one, it was the windowsill of the little white cottage at the end, where a man named Gus repaired clocks.

The cat liked the clock repair window very much. Inside, there were dozens of clocks on the walls and shelves, and they all ticked at slightly different speeds, so that the whole room was full of a soft, uneven pattering, like gentle rain on a roof. Gus worked at a bench by the window with a tiny screwdriver and a lamp, and sometimes he would look up and nod at the cat through the glass, and she would close her eyes and listen to the ticking until she fell asleep.

She always slept for exactly the right amount of time. When she woke, the sunny spot had moved, and so did she.

In the afternoon, the children came home from school, and the cat made herself available. She did not like to be picked up, but she allowed her ears to be scratched, and she allowed herself to be told about spelling tests and playground games and a very interesting worm that someone had found near the fence. She listened to all of it with her eyes half closed, purring softly, and every child on the street went home believing that the cat had understood every word.

Perhaps she had.

At four o'clock, there was tea at Mrs. Lowe's. It was not a real tea party. It was just Mrs. Lowe, a pot of tea, a plate of shortbread, and the cat on the opposite chair, where a guest would sit. Mrs. Lowe talked about her sister, and her roses, and the funny shape of a cloud she had seen that morning. The cat listened, and blinked, and now and then washed one paw in a thoughtful sort of way.

Then the light began to change.

The shadows grew long across the street. The air turned cool and soft and smelled of cut grass and someone's dinner cooking. One by one, the lamps came on in the windows again, the same lamps that had come on that morning, as if the day were folding itself up neatly at both ends.

The cat made her evening rounds. She checked each house one last time. She sat for a moment on each front step, looked at each door, and moved on. Rosie waved to her from an upstairs window, already in her pajamas. Mr. Abbott was closing his garden gate. Gus was switching off the lamp on his workbench, and in the dark shop, all the clocks went on ticking softly to themselves.

When she was quite sure that everyone was home, and fed, and safe, and settling down, the cat went back to the low stone wall at the end of the street.

She sat there with her paws tucked under her, the white tip of her tail curled around her feet, and she watched the last light fade from the sky. The first star came out over the rooftops. Then another.

Then, very quietly, she went to the yellow house with the porch swing, where Mrs. Lowe always left the back door open just a crack. She slipped inside, and climbed onto the soft old armchair by the fire, and turned around three times, and curled up into a small gray circle.

Elm Lane was in order.

And the cat, at last, went off duty, and slept.

stories.title: The Night Train
stories.text:
The train left the city at nine in the evening, from the far end of a long platform under a great curved roof of glass and iron. It was an old train, painted dark green with a thin gold line along its side, and it hissed softly as it waited, like a kettle just before it starts to sing.

June had a ticket for the sleeper car. She had never ridden a night train before, and she had been looking forward to it for weeks.

Her compartment was small and neat, like a cabinet made for a person. There was a narrow bed, already made with crisp white sheets and a thick wool blanket the color of plums. A little folding table under the window. A small lamp with a fringed shade. A hook for a coat, a shelf for a bag, and a tiny sink in the corner with a mirror above it that was hung just slightly too high.

June put her bag on the shelf, hung her coat on the hook, and sat down on the edge of the bed. And the train began to move.

It started so gently she barely noticed. A small jolt, a long creak, and then the platform was sliding slowly past the window, and the lights of the station drifted away behind them, and the train was rolling out into the evening.

For a while, the city went by. Rows of lit windows in tall buildings. A bridge over a dark river, with lamps reflected in the water like long gold ribbons. A busy road, with cars waiting at a crossing, their headlights all turned toward the train as if they had come to wave goodbye.

Then the city began to thin out. The buildings became smaller and farther apart. There were gardens, and sheds, and a church steeple with a single light at the top. And then there was nothing but dark fields, and the occasional farmhouse with one yellow window, and the long, low shape of hills against a sky that still held a little blue at its edges.

There was a soft knock at the door.

June opened it, and there stood the conductor. He was a round, kindly man with a neat white mustache and a dark blue uniform with brass buttons, and he was pushing a small wooden cart. On the cart were a big silver pot, a stack of white cups, a tin of biscuits, and a little jar of marshmallows.

"Good evening," he said. "My name is Mr. Ambrose. Cocoa?"

"Yes, please," said June.

Mr. Ambrose poured the cocoa slowly and carefully, so that not a drop spilled, even as the train swayed. He added two marshmallows without asking, and then, after looking at June for a moment, a third. He placed two biscuits on a little napkin beside the cup.

"First time on the night train?" he asked.

"Is it that obvious?"

"Only a little," said Mr. Ambrose. "First timers always look out the window as if they're afraid they'll miss something."

"Will I?"

Mr. Ambrose smiled under his mustache. "Not really," he said. "That's the nice thing about the night train. There's nothing to miss. There's only the going."

He wished her good night and moved on down the corridor, and June heard him knock softly at the next door, and say good evening, and offer cocoa again.

She sat by the window with the cup warming her hands and watched the dark country go by.

The sound of the train was like nothing else. A steady rhythm of wheels on the rails, clickety clack, clickety clack, over and over, never hurrying, never stopping. Underneath it, a deep, low hum. And every so often, far ahead, the long soft call of the whistle as the train passed a sleeping village or a lonely crossing.

The motion was gentle. A slow sway from side to side, like a boat on a calm lake, or like being rocked.

Around eleven, she went for a walk down the corridor. It was narrow and carpeted, with little lamps along the walls, and it was very quiet. Most of the compartment doors were closed. Behind one, someone was snoring softly. Behind another, someone was listening to a radio play, and she heard a faint voice say something about the weather in a small mountain town.

At the end of the corridor was the lounge car. It had big windows and soft armchairs and little tables with lamps on them. There was only one other person there, an elderly woman with silver hair and a pair of reading glasses on a chain, who was knitting something long and blue.

The woman looked up and smiled. "Can't sleep?" she asked.

"I don't want to yet," said June. "It feels like a waste."

The woman laughed softly. "I've taken this train every autumn for thirty years," she said, "and I still feel exactly the same way."

Her name was Mrs. Hale, and she was knitting a scarf for her grandson. She said it was the longest scarf she had ever knitted, partly because her grandson was very tall, and partly because she kept forgetting to stop. She held it up, and it spilled off her lap and halfway across the floor of the lounge car, and they both laughed quietly, so as not to wake anyone.

They sat together for a while. Mrs. Hale knitted, and her needles made a soft clicking sound that somehow fit perfectly with the clicking of the rails. June watched the window. Outside, the moon had come up, round and pale, and it lit the fields in silver, and the train's long shadow ran along beside them like a faithful dog keeping pace.

At about one in the morning, the train slowed down and stopped at a small station.

It was a tiny place. A single wooden platform, a little station house with a peaked roof, one lamp on a tall post, and a bench. Nobody got on. Nobody got off. A stationmaster in a long coat stepped out of the little house, lifted his lantern, and looked up and down the train. A gray cat sat on the bench beside him, watching too.

Then the stationmaster gave a small wave, and the whistle sounded, soft and far away, and the train began to roll again, and the little station slid away into the dark behind them.

June found that she was smiling, though she could not have said exactly why.

"I always look forward to that stop," said Mrs. Hale. "Nothing ever happens there. It's lovely."

Soon after, June said good night and made her way back along the swaying corridor to her compartment. She washed her face in the tiny sink. She changed into her pajamas. She climbed into the narrow bed and pulled the plum colored blanket up to her chin.

The bed rocked gently. The wheels went on, clickety clack, clickety clack. She left the blind up just a little, so she could see a thin strip of moonlit country going by.

Somewhere ahead there were mountains, and a lake, and a town she had never seen, where someone would be waiting on the platform with a warm coat and a cheerful wave.

But that was the morning. And the morning was a long, long way down the track.

For now there was only the soft dark, and the rocking, and the steady, patient rhythm of the rails, carrying her onward, mile after mile, through the quiet and sleeping world.

stories.title: The Library After Closing
stories.text:
The public library in the middle of town closed at eight o'clock every evening. At five minutes to eight, the head librarian, Mrs. Darby, would ring a small brass bell and say, in her soft but carrying voice, "The library is closing, friends. Please bring your books to the front desk."

And slowly, the readers would gather themselves up. Students closed their notebooks. A man who had been asleep in the newspaper corner woke up and folded his paper neatly, as though he had been reading it the whole time. A mother collected two small children from the rug in the picture book corner, along with a very tall stack of picture books.

By a quarter past eight, the doors were locked, the lights in the reading room were dimmed, and Mrs. Darby had put on her coat and her scarf and gone home.

At nine, Henry arrived.

Henry was the night custodian. He was a quiet man in his sixties, with gentle hands and gray hair that stuck up a little at the back no matter what he did with it. He had been looking after the library at night for nearly twenty years. He had his own key to the side door, his own hook for his coat, and his own mug in the staff room, a big brown one with a small chip on the handle.

He liked the library best at night.

During the day, it was full of rustling and whispering and the soft beep of the checkout machine. But at night, it became something else. The tall shelves stood in long, shadowy rows like trees in a quiet forest. The big windows let in the blue light of the streetlamps. The old radiators along the walls ticked and sighed as they cooled. And the whole building seemed to settle, the way a house settles after everyone has gone to bed.

Henry began, as he always did, by making a pot of tea.

Then he took his cart, with its mop and its bucket and its duster and its little bottle of polish, and he started on his rounds.

He swept the floor of the entrance hall, where the day's footprints made faint patterns on the tiles. He polished the long wooden reading tables until they shone, and he straightened the chairs, pushing each one in so that it sat exactly in line with its neighbor. He dusted the globe in the reference section and gave it a gentle spin, and watched the oceans and the continents turn slowly past.

He emptied the wastepaper baskets. He wiped the fingerprints from the glass of the display case, where there was an old map of the town and a collection of faded postcards. He picked up a single red mitten from under a table in the children's corner and placed it carefully in the lost and found box, next to a blue umbrella and a library card belonging to someone named Pearl.

By eleven, the rounds were done. And that was when Henry did the thing he liked best of all.

Next to the front desk there was a big wooden returns cart, and on it, every evening, were all the books that people had brought back that day. Mrs. Darby and her helpers would put them back on the shelves in the morning. But at night, they waited there, in a tall, untidy pile.

And Henry read them.

Not all of them, of course. And not all the way through. But he would take his cup of tea, and choose a few books from the cart, and carry them to the big green armchair in the corner by the old fireplace, the one nobody had lit in years. Then he would sit, and switch on the small reading lamp, and open the first one.

Tonight, the first book was about bees. It had lovely drawings of honeycombs, and of bees with their fuzzy golden bodies, and of the little dance that bees do to tell each other where the flowers are. Henry read about the dance twice. He thought it was one of the most sensible ideas he had ever heard.

The second book was a cookbook full of soups. Someone had left a slip of paper in it, marking a recipe for potato and leek soup, and on the paper they had written in pencil, very good, add more pepper. Henry smiled and put the slip back exactly where he had found it, so that the next reader would know.

The third book was a collection of poems, old and soft and slightly yellow, and when he opened it, a pressed flower fell out into his lap. It was a small purple violet, flat and dry and perfectly kept. He held it up in the lamplight. Somebody, some time ago, had picked it on a spring day and tucked it between these pages, and it had been traveling quietly from reader to reader ever since.

Henry did not know whether to leave it in or take it out. In the end, he put it back between the same two pages, very gently, and closed the book. It seemed to him that the violet had found a good home, and that it was not his place to move it.

The fourth book was a picture book about a bear who could not fall asleep. The bear tried counting stars, and then counting sheep, and then counting the leaves on a tree, and kept losing count and having to start again. In the end, the bear's mother simply sat beside him and hummed, and he fell asleep before she had finished the song. Henry read it slowly, turning the big pages one by one, and when he got to the end, he sat for a while with the book open on his knees.

Outside, it had started to rain. Very softly. He could hear it on the high windows, a faint, steady pattering, and in the gutters, a gentle trickle.

The radiators ticked. The tall shelves stood quietly in the blue half light. Somewhere in the building, a clock struck one, slow and low.

Henry put the four books back on the cart, each one exactly where it had been. He washed his big brown mug and set it upside down on the draining board. He made one last walk through the library, down the long aisles, past history and gardening and travel and mysteries, past the children's corner with its rug and its beanbags, and back to the front desk.

Everything was in its place. The tables shone. The chairs sat in their neat rows. The returns cart waited for the morning, carrying its quiet cargo of bees and soup and poems and a sleepy bear.

Henry put on his coat. He switched off the small reading lamp by the green armchair. And for a moment, before he left, he stood in the doorway and looked back at the dark reading room, at the long rows of books, all those stories resting side by side on their shelves, waiting patiently for someone to come and open them.

"Good night," he said softly.

Then he locked the side door behind him and walked home through the rain, under his umbrella, along the quiet shining streets, humming a little tune he could not quite remember the end of.

outro: And that is the end of tonight's stories. Let your breathing slow. Let the quiet settle around you, like a warm blanket. The laundromat is humming, the light is turning over the sea, the bread is cooling, the cat is curled up by the fire, the train is rolling on, and the library is resting in the rain. There are more stories waiting here on the channel, whenever you need them. But for now, rest. Good night, and sleep well.
description:
Six cozy, original bedtime stories for grown-ups, read slowly to help you relax and drift off.
A midnight laundromat, a lighthouse keeper and his opinionated gull, a baker on a snowy night, a cat who runs her street, an overnight train, and a library after closing.
No cliffhangers, no drama. Just warm light, soft rain and quiet places.
Lights down, eyes closed. Sweet dreams from Snortlo 🌙
